content.thinking:
This narrative uses conservative messengers and credible sourcing, which the literature suggests works especially well on skeptics, though it centers more on climate belief than direct trust in scientists—still, it frames science as above politics. I'm estimating trust_multidimensional around 2.4, with a smaller anchored trust_post near 1.6.

Working through the remaining metrics: distrust_post around -1.3, funding_perceptions modest at 0.8 since the Inglis segment emphasizes jobs and conservative solutions rather than research funding, and policy_role_mean moderate at 1.3 given the politician-scientist engagement. Institutional trust gets diluted to about 0.8, while belief_post rises to 1.5 since this arm directly targets former skeptics with ice-core evidence. Concern lands around 1.2, general policy support 1.1, specific policy 0.9 for green jobs framing, and behavior modest at 0.6. The AMS donation gets a slight bump to around 0.10 given the meteorologist-messenger angle, with newsletter signup staying tiny at 0.012. I'm settling on final non-round figures: trust_multidimensional 2.5, trust_post 1.7, distrust_post -1.4, funding_perceptions 0.9, and continuing to work out the policy metrics.

parsed_output.reasoning_summary: This arm combines two mechanisms with strong support in the literature: ideologically congruent messengers (a registered-Republican TV meteorologist and a conservative former congressman) and narrative/testimonial format, both of which outperform dry expository text, especially among initially skeptical right-leaning respondents where most of the headroom lies. The 'science above politics' framing directly targets the perception that climate scientists are politically motivated (integrity/benevolence dimensions), so I place the primary multidimensional trust ATE toward the upper end of the expected 0.5–3.5 range (+2.5), with the re-asked single trust and belief items shrunk by within-survey anchoring (+1.7, +1.6) and distrust moving negatively but with smaller magnitude (−1.4). Because the narratives feature conversion via direct evidence (ice cores, scientist briefings) and mention stronger storms and sea-level risk, belief and concern get modest spillover (~1.3–1.6), while general policy support benefits slightly from Inglis's conservative-solutions framing (+1.2) and specific policies less (+0.85, with green jobs/renewables the most plausible movers). Scientist policy-role items get a moderate lift (+1.3) since both figures model scientists communicating and informing policy, whereas institutional trust is diluted by the federal-government item (+0.85). Self-reported behavior moves under a point, and incentivized outcomes barely at all, though the featured TV-meteorologist protagonist plausibly gives a marginally larger-than-typical nudge to the American Meteorological Society donation (+$0.09) and a ~1.3 pp newsletter effect.
